summary: A comic pilgrimage of hunger, fear, pride, play, and frustration, in which the mind-monkey's anger and effort are disciplined into enlightenment.

need-to-breathe.why: Wukong survives forty-nine days in Laozi's furnace by hiding under the wind trigram, his eyes reddened by smoke, and the pilgrims cross monster-haunted rivers, but breath is rarely at stake.

hungry.why: Pigsy's bottomless belly is a running joke, the pilgrims beg alms at every village, Wukong gorges on the peaches of immortality, and every demon hungers to eat Sanzang's flesh.

full.why: Pigsy swallows the ginseng fruit whole and begs for more, and Wukong, bloated on heavenly peaches and Laozi's elixir, staggers drunk from the feast.

thirsty.why: Sanzang and Pigsy drink from the Mother-and-Child River and conceive, and the pilgrims cross dry stretches, but thirst itself is rarely pressing.

gassy.why: Pigsy's body is a source of comedy, but the novel's humor does not reach to gas.

need-to-poop.why: Defecation never figures, even in Pigsy's comedy.

need-to-pee.why: Wukong urinates at the foot of what he takes for a pillar of heaven, really Buddha's finger, and the pilgrims pass their urine to the Taoists of Cart-Slow Kingdom as holy water.

sleepy.why: Pigsy, sent to scout the way, curls up in the grass and sleeps, and Wukong catches him at it more than once.

nauseous.why: Sanzang and Pigsy, pregnant from the river water, groan with bellyache and nausea, and demons retch when Wukong tumbles about inside their stomachs.

dizzy.why: Wukong's cloud-somersault and the pilgrims' tumbles into traps bring moments of reeling, but dizziness is incidental.

fatigued.why: The fourteen-year trek wears Sanzang down at every mountain, and Pigsy grumbles endlessly about the weight of the luggage.

pain.why: Each time Sanzang recites the fillet spell, the golden band bites into Wukong's skull and he writhes on the ground, and demons are beaten to pulp by his staff.

disgusted.why: Demons plan to steam and eat Sanzang, the spider women spin webs from their navels, and Pigsy wallows in filth, snot, and gluttony.

itchy.why: Wukong's monkey fidgeting is noted, but no itch is described.

over-stimulated.why: Wukong's eyes, reddened in Laozi's furnace, water and fail whenever a demon blows smoke at him, and the Flaming Mountain's glare drives the pilgrims back.

too-hot-too-cold.why: The Flaming Mountain's fires scorch the road, forcing Wukong's three attempts to borrow Princess Iron Fan's palm-leaf fan, and Laozi's furnace bakes him for forty-nine days.

afraid.why: Sanzang falls from his horse in terror at every demon, Pigsy wants to divide the luggage and go home, and heaven's hosts quake before the Great Sage.

anxious.why: Sanzang frets at each mountain that monsters wait ahead, and the pilgrims worry through the long road about whether the scriptures will ever be reached.

panic.why: Sanzang shrieks and tumbles from his horse when demons seize him, Pigsy flees fights, and demons scatter in panic when Wukong reveals himself.

sensory-pleasures.why: Wukong feasts on heavenly peaches and immortal wine, Pigsy delights in every meal, and the Queen of Women's Kingdom tempts Sanzang with a bridal banquet.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The novel pauses to admire mountains, monasteries, and Guanyin's embroidered cassock, which the aged abbot Jinchi covets so much he tries to burn the pilgrims for it.

fun-excitement.why: Wukong revels in mischief, transforming into insects and temples, tricking Pigsy and demons, and treats battle itself as play from the Water Curtain Cave onward.

orgasm.why: Pigsy lusts and demonesses try to bed Sanzang, but no act is consummated; the monk keeps his primal yang.

love-romantic.why: The Queen of Women's Kingdom proposes marriage to Sanzang, Pigsy is wed to Squire Gao's daughter, and the Bull Demon King quarrels with Princess Iron Fan over his concubine.

love-family.why: Princess Iron Fan hates Wukong for taking her son Red Boy, the Bull Demon King fights for his family, and Wukong treats his monkeys at Flower-Fruit Mountain as kin.

grief.why: Wukong weeps when Sanzang banishes him after the White Bone Demon, and returns to find Flower-Fruit Mountain burned and his monkeys hunted.

missing-someone.why: Banished to Flower-Fruit Mountain, Wukong looks east and weeps for his master, and Sanzang, captured, wishes aloud for the disciple he drove away.

aroused-sexually.why: Pigsy, banished from heaven for molesting the moon goddess, lusts after every woman he meets and is trussed up by the Bodhisattvas' test, while demonesses crave Sanzang's yang.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The four pilgrims bicker and rescue one another for fourteen years, Wukong and Pigsy taunt each other like brothers, and Wukong once swore brotherhood with the Bull Demon King.

empathy.why: Sanzang feels for every beggar, child, and old woman the demons impersonate, which is exactly how they trap him.

compassion.why: Sanzang's mercy toward every stranger, Guanyin's interventions, and Wukong's rescues of kingdoms, children, and captives make compassion the pilgrimage's purpose.

grateful.why: Wukong kowtows to Sanzang for freeing him from the mountain, rescued kings and villagers feast the pilgrims, and Sanzang is bound to Taizong by sworn brotherhood.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Wukong delights in ridding kingdoms of demons and freeing captives, boasting of each rescue, though the boast matters to him more than the helping.

trustful-distrustful.why: Sanzang refuses to believe Wukong that the old woman is the White Bone Demon, demons deceive the pilgrims by disguise in episode after episode, and the Six-Eared Macaque fools even heaven.

depressed.why: Wukong under Five Elements Mountain for five hundred years begs each passerby for release, and Sanzang in demon cages weeps that his quest is doomed.

angry.why: Wukong wrecks heaven over the insult of being made stable boy, rages at Sanzang's unfairness, and bullies Pigsy; Sanzang in turn storms at Wukong's killings.

envious.why: Wukong rebels because he is left off the Peach Banquet guest list, Pigsy envies the credit Wukong gets, and Abbot Jinchi covets the cassock.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Princess Iron Fan resents the Bull Demon King's new concubine, the Jade-Faced Fox, but romantic jealousy is otherwise absent.

jealous-friendship.why: Pigsy, jealous of Wukong's favor with the master, eggs Sanzang on to banish him after the White Bone Demon.

hatred.why: Princess Iron Fan hates Wukong for taking her son and fans him away three times, and the demons of every mountain want his blood.

contempt.why: Heaven makes the monkey a stable boy, Wukong calls the Jade Emperor an old fool and Pigsy an idiot, and Pigsy sneers back at the monkey.

resentment.why: Wukong rebels against heaven's slights, resents Sanzang's unjust fillet spells, and Pigsy grumbles that he carries the luggage while Wukong takes the credit.

proud.why: Wukong styles himself Great Sage Equal to Heaven, boasts of his seventy-two transformations before every demon, and bets Buddha he can leap out of his palm.

amused.why: Wukong's taunts, Pigsy's humiliations, and the pilgrims' deflating of pompous gods and demons keep the novel comic from first chapter to last.

sense-of-belonging.why: Wukong demands a place among the gods and is denied, finds one among the pilgrims, and all five are enrolled among the Buddhas at the end.

lonely.why: Wukong spends five hundred years alone under Five Elements Mountain, and Sandy haunts the Flowing Sands River alone, eating travelers.

judgy-moral-sense.why: Sanzang condemns Wukong's killing of the White Bone Demon as murder of innocents, heaven tries and sentences the rebel monkey, and demons are judged and punished in each episode.

admiration.why: The monkeys worship Wukong as king, Sanzang reveres Guanyin and Buddha, and the kings they free honor the pilgrims.

embarrassed.why: Pigsy is strung up in a tree by the Bodhisattvas disguised as a mother and daughters after trying to marry all of them, and Sanzang and Pigsy carry demon-river pregnancies.

shame.why: Wukong is mortified to learn his heavenly post is the lowest in the stables, and Pigsy is ashamed of the pig face that frightens his bride.

guilt.why: Sanzang regrets banishing Wukong when demons catch him, and Pigsy confesses his failings each time he is caught sleeping or lusting.

sad.why: Sanzang weeps at each capture and at each mountain ahead, and Wukong sheds tears at banishment, but sorrow passes quickly in a comic novel.

happy.why: Wukong's early reign over the monkeys in Water Curtain Cave is a carefree paradise, and the pilgrims are at ease in hospitable monasteries.

joyful-euphoric.why: Wukong whoops with triumph at each demon beaten and at his elixir-fuelled immortality, and the pilgrims rejoice on reaching Vulture Peak and receiving the scriptures.

effort.why: The pilgrimage is fourteen years and eighty-one ordeals of effort, with Pigsy forever proposing to quit and Wukong forever pushing on.

focused-in-flow.why: Wukong absorbs Subodhi's teachings and the seventy-two transformations in rapt practice, and loses himself in combat with every demon.

bored.why: Wukong, made Great Sage with no duties, wanders heaven in boredom until he raids the peach garden, and Pigsy dozes through every lull.

distracted.why: Pigsy forgets his errands at the sight of food or a woman, and Wukong is lured from Sanzang's side by demons' diversions.

impatient.why: Wukong chafes at Sanzang's timidity and the plodding pace, and Pigsy cannot wait for a meal to be served before grabbing it.

curious.why: Wukong leaps through the waterfall to find the Water Curtain Cave, sails the seas seeking immortality, and probes every demon's lair for its secret.

surprised.why: The pilgrims find the first scriptures blank, Sanzang is startled when kind old women turn out to be demons, and demons gape when the captive monk's disciple pops out of their belly.

awe.why: Wukong somersaults to the end of the world and finds he never left Buddha's palm, and the pilgrims are awed by Vulture Peak and the Buddha's assembly.

skeptical-doubtful.why: Wukong's fiery eyes see through every disguise while Sanzang doubts him, and Wukong suspects the blank scriptures are a swindle by the disciples who demanded a bribe.

feeling-of-knowing.why: Wukong often senses that a demon is something he has met in heaven, and goes to the gods to find out whose escaped pet or servant it is.

confused.why: Neither Sanzang, Guanyin, nor the Jade Emperor can tell the true Wukong from the Six-Eared Macaque, and the pilgrims are baffled by demons' illusions and false Buddhas.

frustrated.why: Wukong fails three times to get Princess Iron Fan's fan, cannot beat Red Boy's fire or the Bull Demon's strength alone, and is driven wild by the fillet and his master's gullibility.

uncertain-certain.why: Sanzang wavers between Wukong's warnings and Pigsy's insinuations, and the pilgrims hesitate at every river and mountain road.

understanding.why: Wukong grasps the Heart Sutra's emptiness before his master does, and at the end all understand that the blank scriptures were the true ones for those who could read them.

inspired.why: Wukong hits on turning himself into a tiny fly, a demon's wife, or a temple, and on the trick of tumbling about inside a monster's stomach.

satisfied.why: After the eighty-first ordeal the pilgrims deliver the scriptures to Taizong and are made Buddhas and arhats, and Wukong's fillet vanishes at last.

foreboding.why: Sanzang grows uneasy at every dark mountain, and Guanyin's prophecy of eighty-one ordeals hangs over the road.

nostalgia.why: Wukong looks back to his carefree days as Monkey King of Flower-Fruit Mountain, and Sanzang longs for the Tang court.

anticipation-suspense.why: Each episode hangs on whether Wukong can rescue Sanzang before the demon's steamer is ready.

hope.why: The pilgrims press on for fourteen years hoping to reach Thunderclap Monastery, and Wukong hopes for freedom from the mountain and from the fillet.

schadenfreude.why: Wukong laughs at Pigsy strung up in a tree and pregnant, and Pigsy gloats when the fillet spell sends Wukong rolling; each relishes the other's misfortunes.

elevation.why: Guanyin's interventions and Sanzang's unbending mercy, even toward demons, offer moments of moral uplift.

infatuation.why: Pigsy falls for every pretty face, and the Scorpion Demon and the Queen of Women are infatuated with Sanzang.

rage.why: Wukong's havoc in heaven is rage unleashed, and Princess Iron Fan's rage at the loss of Red Boy sends Wukong flying with her fan.
